flawed_step: Line 0011: "I therefore chose a value $c_1$ that respect the condition $0 \le M \le c_1$ in order to define the relation $0 \le c_1 g(n) \le f(n)$" (and, relatedly, the total absence of any argument for $f(n) \neq O(g(n))$, which lines 0017-0020 explicitly leave open).
counterexample: The inequality in line 0011 points the wrong way. From line 0010 we have f(n) > M*g(n) for all n >= n_0. To conclude c_1*g(n) <= f(n) one needs c_1 <= M; the proof instead requires M <= c_1, which does not license the conclusion. Concrete instance: f(n) = n^2, g(n) = n, so f/g = n -> infinity. Take M = 1; then n_0 = 2 works, since f(n) = n^2 > 1*n = M*g(n) for all n >= 2. Now choose c_1 = 100, which satisfies the proof's stated condition 0 <= M <= c_1 (0 <= 1 <= 100). The claimed relation 0 <= c_1*g(n) <= f(n) then reads 100n <= n^2, which is FALSE for every n with 2 <= n <= 99 -- e.g. at n = 10, c_1*g(10) = 100*10 = 1000 while f(10) = 100, so 1000 <= 100 fails. Hence the stated choice rule for c_1 does not produce a valid Omega witness at any n >= n_0; the step is a non sequitur (the correct choice is any 0 < c_1 <= M).
reasoning_summary: The submitted text is an SE question, not a completed proof: it argues only the Omega direction and then explicitly asks how to prove f(n) != O(g(n)) (lines 0015-0020), so the second half of the claimed statement is unproved. Moreover the Omega half is itself broken at line 0011, where the author picks c_1 with M <= c_1 and asserts c_1*g(n) <= f(n). From f(n) > M*g(n) this gives nothing: multiplying g by a LARGER constant makes the lower bound harder, not easier. Explicit refutation of that inference: f(n)=n^2, g(n)=n, M=1, n_0=2, c_1=100 satisfies the proof's own condition yet 100n <= n^2 fails throughout 2 <= n <= 99 (n=10: 1000 <= 100 is false). The valid argument needs c_1 <= M (e.g. c_1 = M = 1), the opposite constraint. Also unstated is the hypothesis g(n) > 0 needed to multiply through in line 0010. Verdict: INVALID.
